checklist.name: ml-genomics-failures
checklist.title: Book of failures: ML in genomics
checklist.summary: A catalogue of ways ML-in-genomics results have been inflated or misread, each with the test that exposes it. Run the audit before you trust a metric, and before you write a conclusion that says a model "learned biology".
checklist.description: Book of failures for machine learning on genomic and biological data - documented cases where a model looked good but had learned a shortcut, leaked test data, or was never compared to a simple baseline. Use it to audit an ML experiment, benchmark, evaluation split, control or paper claim in genomics, transcriptomics, single-cell, regulatory genomics, variant effect prediction, gene regulatory networks, DNA/protein language models or genotype-to-phenotype models. Trigger on "does it learn something biological", "is this result real", "why does the control also work", "review this evaluation", "design a train/test split", "what baselines do we need", "is this leakage", or before reporting any held-out metric.

classes.name: Leakage through shared entities
classes.test: Does any test example share a gene, enhancer, promoter, species, individual, homologous sequence or batch with training?

classes.name: Shortcut / confounder
classes.test: Can a trivial feature (distance, GC, gene degree, phylogeny, batch, ancestry, depth) predict the label alone?

classes.name: Wrong axis of generalization
classes.test: Does the test vary the same thing the claim is about (across individuals vs across genes, across phenotypes vs across lineages)?

classes.name: Missing or weak baseline
classes.test: Has it been compared with mean, linear, nearest-neighbour, one-hot CNN and k-mer baselines?

classes.name: Circular evaluation
classes.test: Were benchmark labels, or the tools that made them, also used in training?

classes.name: Control that isn't a null
classes.test: What does the ablation keep? If it keeps the confounder, a good score under the control proves nothing.

audit.intro: Answer each question in writing, with numbers from the run where possible.

steps.title: Unit of independence
steps.text: What is one independent example: a pair, a gene, a species, a person or a locus? Split at that level, or above it. Random splits of pairs, edges, windows or photos almost always leak (L).

steps.title: Shortcut inventory
steps.text: List every non-biological or coarse feature that correlates with the label. Fit a model on each one alone. If one of them reaches most of the headline score, the headline is about that feature (S).

steps.title: Claim vs test axis
steps.text: Write the claim as "X predicts Y across Z". Check that the held-out set varies Z, with the confounder held fixed (A).

steps.title: Baselines
steps.text: Report the cheapest baselines next to the model: chance, the label prior, per-entity means, linear/additive models, nearest neighbour on a simple representation (k-mers, one-hot CNN, highly variable genes) (B).

steps.title: A true null
steps.text: Run at least one control that should drop the score to chance, such as permuting labels at the entity level or giving each entity another entity's input. If the null doesn't fall to chance, something leaks (K).

steps.title: What does each control keep?
steps.text: For every ablation, write down which information survives it. A control that keeps the main confounder isn't evidence either way (K).

steps.title: Circularity
steps.text: Trace where the benchmark labels came from. Remove anything that shares origin with the training data (C).

steps.title: Variance
steps.text: One seed and a few dozen held-out entities can't separate effects of a few points. Give counts ("25/30 species"), not only rates.

usage: Match the experiment to cases by class code and domain, and cite them by ID (e.g. `F03`).
Treat each case as a hypothesis to test on the current run, not a verdict. Say which check would confirm it.
Quote sources as listed. Don't add claims about a paper that the case doesn't contain. Read the paper first.

cases.title: Genome → organism image learns phylogeny, not phenotype
cases.domain: Genotype-to-phenotype; DNA language model (ModernGENA) aligned to BioCLIP image space, decoded with Stable Diffusion (genes.jpg).
cases.claim: From random 6.3 kb nuclear-genome windows, the model places held-out species in the right family (25/30 held-out mammals, family top-1 0.83) and generates images that look like the organism.
cases.mechanism: Each species has one genome, so the training target is effectively a species label. The loss also includes a taxonomy-caption term, and BioCLIP's image space is organized by taxonomy. The model learns "which lineage is this genome from" and returns its nearest training relative's appearance. Nothing tests whether DNA predicts phenotype beyond what phylogeny already predicts.
red_flags: Accuracy degrades by taxonomic distance, not by trait: new species from a known family 0.83 family top-1, new families 0.00 at family and order level (class only).
Generated images show the nearest relative: horse → zebras, black rhino → elephants.
A frozen-embedding ridge regression gets 0.53–0.58 species top-1 on seen species and 0.00 on new ones: seen-species scores are memorization.
A composition-only k-mer nearest neighbour already gets 0.67 family top-1 on new species.
cases.test: A nearest-relative baseline using true phylogenetic distance (tree distance, Mash/ANI) that returns the relative's photos. Score traits (body size, habitat, colour) and test whether DNA explains the variation left after phylogeny (phylogenetic contrasts). Look at lineages where phenotype breaks from phylogeny (whales vs hippos, seals).
cases.fix: Report results as phylogenetic signal unless they beat the phylogeny baseline. Use phenotype-relevant input (coding sequences, candidate genes) rather than random windows, which are about 1–2% coding in mammals. A potential approach is to use domain knowledge and measured biological signals to define and supervise an intermediate layer between DNA and phenotype: predict gene expression, chromatin states or other functional features in relevant tissues and developmental stages, then use those predictions to predict phenotype. Validate the intermediate predictions independently and test whether they improve phenotype prediction beyond the phylogeny baseline; adding this layer alone does not establish that the model learned phenotype.

sources.citation: Felsenstein J. Phylogenies and the comparative method. Am Nat 125:1–15 (1985).

status.pending: Genome-permutation null (control C) prepared, not trained; phylogeny baseline not built.

cases.title: Token-order shuffle mistaken for a null control
cases.claim: "The shuffled-DNA control still performs well, so something is wrong" or, conversely, "the model beats the shuffled control, so it reads DNA order / biology".
cases.mechanism: Shuffling BPE tokens within a window (about 6 bp per token at 1024 tokens / 6.3 kb) keeps the bag of tokens, roughly a 6-mer composition spectrum. Composition (GC, k-mer bias, repeat content) carries phylogeny, so the shuffled model reaches about the k-mer baseline. It's an order ablation, not a null. The gap between intact and shuffled input is also confounded: shuffled tokens are out of distribution for the pretrained LM, so they may just be harder to fine-tune. And "order" signal can still be phylogenetic (structure of lineage-specific transposable elements and satellites, ~50% of a mammal genome), not genes.
red_flags: The shuffled control lands near a composition baseline.
Its loss is still falling at the end of training.
The frozen pretrained baseline doesn't change under shuffling.
cases.test: Run a true null alongside (each entity gets another entity's input; held-out scores should fall to chance). Compare shuffled vs intact at matched training loss and over several seeds. Restrict windows to repeat-masked or coding regions to see where the order signal comes from.
cases.fix: Label each control by what it removes and what it keeps. Only call a control a null if it removes the confounder too.

sources.citation: genes.jpg control B report (shuffled 16/30 vs intact 25/30 family top-1 on held-out species; k-mer baseline 20/30; one seed).

status.pending: Multi-seed and matched-loss comparison not run.

cases.title: Enhancer–promoter interaction prediction inflated by shared elements
cases.domain: Regulatory genomics; predicting which enhancer–promoter (EP) pairs interact (e.g. TargetFinder and later methods).
cases.claim: High accuracy at telling interacting from non-interacting EP pairs using epigenomic features or sequence.
cases.mechanism: Pairs were split at random, so the same enhancers and promoters appeared in both training and test pairs. The test set wasn't independent of training, and models could memorize element-level properties (e.g. how often an element interacts) instead of learning interactions. Performance fell sharply under splits that keep elements, or chromosomes, apart. Xi & Beer also found that the high accuracy came largely from features of the window between enhancer and promoter, and that local epigenomic state alone discriminated poorly.
red_flags: Pair-level random cross-validation.
A high score from features that describe one element only.
Positive and negative pairs with different distance distributions.
cases.test: Split by chromosome or by element, so no enhancer or promoter is on both sides. Run a baseline using only per-element features or only distance.
cases.fix: Entity-level or chromosome-level splits; distance-matched negatives.

sources.citation: Cao F, Fullwood MJ. Inflated performance measures in enhancer–promoter interaction-prediction methods. Nat Genet 51:1196–1198 (2019).
Reply by the TargetFinder authors, acknowledging the non-IID problem. Nat Genet (2019).
Xi W, Beer MA. Local epigenomic state cannot discriminate interacting and non-interacting enhancer–promoter pairs with high accuracy. PLoS Comput Biol 14:e1006625 (2018).

cases.title: Supervised GRN inference learns per-gene label imbalance
cases.domain: Gene regulatory network inference from single-cell expression with supervised models trained on known (ground-truth) TF–target edges.
cases.claim: Supervised models reach high accuracy at predicting regulatory edges.
cases.mechanism: Standard benchmarks hide edges between genes that also appear in training. Models can exploit gene-specific biases such as each gene's class imbalance (how many known interactions it has) instead of learning regulatory mechanisms. On interactions involving genes absent from training, the advantage shrinks.
red_flags: Edge-level random splits.
Most test edges touch hub genes seen in training.
A per-gene degree prior gets close to the model's score.
cases.test: "Unseen genes" split (test genes absent from training). Baseline that scores an edge by its genes' training degree alone.
cases.fix: Evaluate on unseen genes, which is also the realistic use case (e.g. biomarker discovery). InfoSEM uses ground-truth labels as a prior instead of direct supervision, plus textual gene embeddings from foundation models.

sources.citation: Cui T, Xu S-J, Moskalev A, Li S, Mansi T, Prakash M, Liao R. InfoSEM: A deep generative model with informative priors for gene regulatory network inference. arXiv:2503.04483 (2025); ICML 2025.

cases.title: Sequence-to-expression models fail across individuals
cases.domain: Sequence-to-expression deep learning (Enformer, Basenji2, ExPecto, Xpresso).
cases.claim: Models that predict expression from DNA sequence well should predict the effect of personal genetic variants on expression.
cases.mechanism: They were trained and evaluated on variation across genes (on the reference genome). Applied to personal genomes, they explain little of the variation across individuals, and often get the direction of a cis-regulatory variant's effect wrong.
red_flags: A claim about variants or individuals backed only by across-gene correlation.
cases.test: Evaluate on paired personal genomes and transcriptomes (e.g. Geuvadis, GTEx), per gene, across individuals, including the sign of the effect.
cases.fix: Make the test vary the same axis as the claim. Train on personal sequence variation where the goal is variant effects.

sources.citation: Huang C, et al. Personal transcriptome variation is poorly explained by current genomic deep learning models. Nat Genet (2023).
Sasse A, et al. Benchmarking of deep neural networks for predicting personal gene expression from DNA sequence highlights shortcomings. Nat Genet 55:2060–2064 (2023).

cases.title: Perturbation-effect models don't beat linear baselines
cases.domain: Predicting transcriptome changes after single or double genetic perturbations (foundation models and other deep learning models).
cases.claim: Deep models predict the outcome of unseen perturbations.
cases.mechanism: Compared against deliberately simple baselines, five foundation models and two other deep models did not outperform them. For double perturbations their error was higher than an additive model's.
red_flags: A comparison only against other deep models.
No mean or additive baseline.
cases.test: Report a no-change/mean baseline, an additive model for combinations, and a linear model next to the deep model.
cases.fix: Make these baselines mandatory in perturbation benchmarks.

sources.citation: Ahlmann-Eltze C, Huber W, Anders S. Deep-learning-based gene perturbation effect prediction does not yet outperform simple linear baselines. Nat Methods 22:1657–1661 (2025).

cases.title: Single-cell foundation models lose to HVG/scVI zero-shot
cases.domain: Single-cell foundation models (Geneformer, scGPT) used without fine-tuning.
cases.claim: Pretrained cell embeddings are useful as they are for clustering and batch integration.
cases.mechanism: Zero-shot, both models performed worse than selecting highly variable genes or using established methods (Harmony, scVI) for cell type clustering and batch integration. They sometimes did worse on datasets that were in their own pretraining data.
red_flags: Results reported only after fine-tuning.
No HVG/PCA/scVI baselines.
cases.test: Zero-shot evaluation against HVG + PCA, Harmony and scVI.
cases.fix: Include those baselines. Don't assume pretraining scale buys generalization.

sources.citation: Kedzierska KZ, et al. Zero-shot evaluation reveals limitations of single-cell foundation models. Genome Biol (2025).

cases.title: DNA language model embeddings don't beat one-hot CNNs
cases.domain: Genomic language models (Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT2, HyenaDNA, GPN) for regulatory genomics tasks.
cases.claim: Pretrained DNA LM representations improve functional genomics prediction.
cases.mechanism: On six cell-type-specific regulatory tasks, representations from LMs pretrained on whole genomes gave no noticeable advantage over one-hot sequence with a conventional supervised network. Supervised models pretrained on functional genomics data transferred better, when the source and target tasks were close.
red_flags: The LM is compared only with other LMs, or with a weak non-deep baseline.
cases.test: Train a one-hot CNN of similar capacity on the same task and split.
cases.fix: A one-hot CNN baseline is mandatory. A k-mer composition baseline (see F01, F02) shows how much of the signal is composition.

sources.citation: Tang Z, Somia N, Yu Y, Koo PK. Evaluating the representational power of pre-trained DNA language models for regulatory genomics. Genome Biol (2025).

cases.title: Missense pathogenicity benchmarks are circular
cases.claim: Tool X beats others on a pathogenic vs benign missense benchmark.
cases.mechanism: Two kinds of circularity. (1) Benchmark variants overlap with the variants the tools were trained on. (2) Variants in the same gene tend to have the same label, so a tool can score well by learning which genes are pathogenic rather than which variants are.
red_flags: A benchmark drawn from the same databases (e.g. ClinVar, HGMD) used to train the tools.
Genes with only pathogenic or only benign variants.
cases.test: Remove variants seen in any tool's training data. Evaluate within genes that have both labels, or with gene-level splits. Run a baseline using only the gene's label proportion.
cases.fix: Held-out variant sets with documented provenance; gene-balanced evaluation.

sources.citation: Grimm DG, et al. The evaluation of tools used to predict the impact of missense variants is hindered by two types of circularity. Hum Mutat 36:513–523 (2015).

cases.title: Batch effects confounded with the outcome
cases.domain: Any high-throughput assay (microarray, sequencing, proteomics, single-cell).
cases.claim: A classifier separates cases from controls, or one condition from another.
cases.mechanism: Lab conditions, reagent lots, processing date and personnel shift the measurements. When batch is correlated with the outcome, models learn the batch.
red_flags: All cases processed in one batch.
Processing date or plate predicts the label.
Performance falls on an external cohort.
cases.test: Predict the label from batch variables alone. Check whether the top principal components track batch. Validate on data from another batch or site.
cases.fix: Randomize the outcome across batches at design time. Split by batch or site. Correct batch effects within training folds only, so the correction doesn't leak test information.

sources.citation: Leek JT, et al. Tackling the widespread and critical impact of batch effects in high-throughput data. Nat Rev Genet 11:733–739 (2010).

cases.title: Polygenic scores lose accuracy across ancestries
cases.claim: A polygenic score predicts the trait.
cases.mechanism: Scores built from mostly European-ancestry GWAS were several times more accurate in people of European ancestry than in other ancestries. Accuracy measured within one ancestry doesn't carry over to others.
red_flags: Training and test drawn from the same ancestry group.
Population structure correlated with the trait.
cases.test: Report accuracy stratified by ancestry. Evaluate in a cohort of different ancestry.
cases.fix: Diverse training cohorts; report stratified performance; control for population structure.

sources.citation: Martin AR, et al. Clinical use of current polygenic risk scores may exacerbate health disparities. Nat Genet 51:584–591 (2019).

cases.title: Homologous sequences on both sides of the split
cases.domain: Any model trained on DNA, RNA or protein sequences.
cases.claim: The model generalizes to new sequences.
cases.mechanism: Random splits put near-identical sequences (paralogs, orthologs, repeats, close homologs) in both training and test, so test accuracy partly measures recall of training examples. Holding out a chromosome doesn't stop this: paralogs and repeat families span chromosomes.
red_flags: No sequence-identity filtering between splits.
Accuracy falls with the test example's distance to its nearest training sequence.
cases.test: For each test sequence, compute identity to its nearest training sequence, and plot accuracy against it.
cases.fix: Cluster by sequence identity (e.g. MMseqs2, CD-HIT) and split by cluster. Report performance by distance to training.

sources.citation: General pitfall ("dependent examples") in Whalen S, Schreiber J, Noble WS, Pollard KS. Navigating the pitfalls of applying machine learning in genomics. Nat Rev Genet 23:169–181 (2022). The review also covers distributional differences, confounding, leaky preprocessing and unbalanced classes, and is the best single reference behind this book.
